Demystifying Data Salaries (Part 2)¶

("salary.jpg")
Source: Google

This project was completed in June, 2025. It is the second of three, all of which use the same dataset.¶

📖 Background¶

You work for an international HR consultancy helping companies attract and retain top talent in the competitive tech industry. As part of your services, you provide clients with insights into industry salary trends to ensure they remain competitive in hiring and compensation practices.

Your team wants to use a data-driven approach to analyse how various factors—such as job role, experience level, remote work, and company size—impact salaries globally. By understanding these trends, you can assist in advising clients on offering competitive packages to attract the best talent.

In this project competition, which consists of three levels or parts, salary data from thousands of employees worldwide will be explored, mined, & visualized. Subsequent levels of this project will involve building predictive models to uncover key salary drivers and providing insights on how to enhance future data collection.

💾 The Data¶

The data, available in salaries.csv, comes from a survey hosted by the aforementioned HR consultancy. Each data point represents a single employee's salary record for a given year.

Column Description
work_year The year the salary was paid.
experience_level Employee experience level. EN: Entry-level / Junior, MI: Mid-level / Intermediate, SE: Senior / Expert, EX: Executive / Director
employment_type Employment type. PT: Part-time, FT: Full-time, CT: Contract, FL: Freelance
job_title The job title during the year.
salary Gross salary paid (in local currency).
salary_currency Salary currency (ISO 4217 code).
salary_in_usd Salary converted to USD using average yearly FX rate.
employee_residence Employee's primary country of residence (ISO 3166 code).
remote_ratio Percentage of remote work. 0: No remote work (<20%), 50: Hybrid (50%), 100: Fully remote (>80%)
company_location Employer's main office location (ISO 3166 code).
company_size Company size. S: Small (<50 employees), M: Medium (50–250 employees), L: Large (>250 employees)

💪 Competition challenge¶

In this second level, you’ll create visualisations to analyse the data and uncover trends. Create a report that answers the following.

  • Create a bar chart displaying the top 5 job titles with the highest average salary (in USD).
  • Compare the average salaries for employees working remotely 100%, 50%, and 0%. What patterns or trends are present?
  • Visualise the salary distribution (in USD) across company sizes (S, M, L). Which company size offers the highest average salary?

Objectives¶

1) Create a bar chart displaying the top 5 job titles with the highest average salary (in USD). 2) Compare the average salaries for employees working remotely 100%, 50%, and 0%. What patterns or trends are present? 3) Visualise the salary distribution (in USD) across company sizes (S, M, L). Which company size offers the highest average salary?

Summary of Findings & Recommendations¶

This project (part two of three) analyzed over 57,000 survey responses of individuals within the tech industry regarding their employment details between 2020-2024. As no preprocessing was necessary, the analyses examined specific subsets of individuals & their salaries. In particular, employment & salary information was evaluated based on the top-earning positions, how much employees worked remotely, & the size of their company. In assessing such individuals, a deeper understanding as to some recent/current trends of employees & salaries within the tech industry was uncovered. Such information can be used to assist companies within the industry in attracting the best candidates & to help drive success.

Analysis I - Highest-Paying Jobs¶

Of the 57,194 survey responses, the jobs with the highest average salaries were identified to get a basic understanding as to which positions saw the most pay. To account for less-than-representative job titles, two methods were employed to obtain these job titles.

Firstly, the five jobs with the greatest average salaries across all of the responses were identified & examined. They included (from highest to lowest): Analytics Engineering Manager, Data Science Tech Lead, Applied AI ML Lead, Head of Machine Learning, & Engineering Manager. Their average salaries ranged between \$262,000-\\$400,000. The first three titles had either one or two records each & so it is difficult to weigh the reliability of the associated observations. The latter jobs two had nine & 268 data points respectively, so they are relatively more representative.

Second, the five jobs with the greatest average salaries of those with at least three survey responses were retrieved & analyzed. They included (from highest to lowest): Head of Machine Learning, Engineering Manager, Head of AI, Machine Learning Model Engineer, & Director of Machine Learning. Their average salaries ranged between \$242,000-\\$289,000. While the Head of Machine Learning sees the highest average salary of these jobs, they also see the smallest outright salary & the most volatility. As such, estimating salaries of Machine Learning Heads may be more challenging. The job with the most consistent salaries of these five positions is the Machine Learning Model Engineer. Overall, the more consistent the salaries of these positions, the more reliable & predictable they are for companies who may be looking to hire such positions.

Across both of these methods, there were some commonalities in the positions. Firstly, two of the jobs--Head of Machine Learning & Engineering Manager--directly overlapped. Additionally, of these eight positions, seven of them refer to titles that directly oversee & direct other employees such as managers, leads, heads, or directors. Moreover, three of them relate to engineering, four relate to machine learning (ML), & two relate to artificial intelligence (AI).

As such, managerial jobs across these three fields appear to be particularly specialized & therefore command higher levels of pay within the tech industry. Such jobs are likely to be very competitive because companies will want to make sure that candidates are fully capable & worthy of positions that involve many responsibilities. As a consequence, companies should be willing to offer strong salaries to candidates whom meet their satisfaction in the hiring process.

Analysis II - Remote Work & Average Salary¶

With continuing developments in technology, the ability for people to work fully remotely & remain effective has become more accessible. Although fully-remote work may impact work within the office building of a company or business, such as ease of communication & working environment, this style of work can also improve accessibility for both companies & employees in terms of who they can hire & where they can work respectively. In hiring employees who work fully remotely, companies can have a wider range of candidates whom they can choose from to fill positions. For hybrid work, employees still need to be near their office & so hiring such candidates will still be as restricted as for those who work fully in person.
Ultimately, whether companies prefer fully-remote or in-person work will depend on various factors, but hybrid work will likely require additional resources & levels of accessibility because companies will have to handle people who work both in the office & outside it. As such, hybrid work may be less desirable for businesses.

Reported salaries were analyzed according to how much remote work employees did which was described using three remote ratios. Employees either worked mostly remotely, rarely worked remotely (in person), or worked evenly between remote work & non-remote work (hybrid). Through analyzing salaries across these remote ratios, trends & differences were obtained that might be indicative as to how popular these three types of work have been & what consequences they might associate with.

Firstly, while there large sample sizes of responses across all three remote ratios, only 271 responses correspond to hybrid employees, whereas the other two ratios each accounted for at least 12,500 responses. Such an imbalance could point to preferences among companies who hire such individuals & the tech industry in general in that hybrid work is not really offered. Alternatively, it could point to a bias in the people who were surveyed in that hybrid workers were not represented equally.

With this established, salaries were aggregated both overall & on an annual basis. Generally, hybrid workers reported salaries (~ \$80,000) that were typically about half of those of either in-person or fully remote employees (~ \\$160,000 & \$150,000 respectively). Such an imbalance may be related to a hiring preferential of companies in that they want candidates to fully commit to one way or the other when it comes to remote work. Over the 2020-2024 period, average salaries of the three remote-work types were within about \\$30,000 of each other; however, by 2024, this difference had grown beyond \$80,000. In particular, average salaries of fully remote & in-person employees grew significantly, whereas that of hybrid employees actually decreased by about \\$5,000.

Given these findings, it is fairly evident that in-person work became increasingly more valuable over these five years. Fully remote work also saw an increase in value but not quite to the same extent. Hybrid work, on the other hand, saw a small decrease in value from 2020-2024. Consequentially, it could be inferred that tech companies generally prioritized in-person & fully remote positions significantly more than hybrid positions. Furthermore, hybrid employees seemingly would generally have had, & might in the near future, more difficulty in obtaining a hybrid position that pays well.

Analysis III - Company Size & Salary¶

Reported salaries were analyzed according to the size of the company employees worked at. Companies were labeled as either small (less than 50 employees), medium (between 50-250 employees), or large (more than 250 employees). Through analyzing salaries across these company sizes, trends & differences were obtained that might be indicative as to how capable &/or conservative companies were when it comes to providing competitive salaries.

Firstly, even though there are more than 200 responses across the three company sizes, only 204 correspond to small companies & 1,965 correspond to medium-size companies. Although this is slightly logical given how the groups were defined, such an imbalance could give a general indication as to the size of most companies within the tech industry. Alternatively, it could point to a bias in the people who were surveyed in that small & large companies were not represented equally to medium-size companies.

With that aside, salaries were aggregated both overall & on an annual basis. Generally, workers from small companies reported salaries (~ \$88,000) that were roughly half of those from medium-size or large companies (~ \\$160,000 & \$153,000 respectively). Such an imbalance may be related to hiring capabilities of companies, their resources, & how they chose to allocate them when it comes to the salaries of their employees. Over the 2020-2024 period, average salaries of the three companies were within roughly \\$37,000 of each other, but this disparity grew to over \$70,000 in 2024. In particular, average salaries of employees from medium-size & large companies grew considerably, whereas those of employees from small companies only increased by about \\$16,000. Moreover, average salaries of those from medium-size & large companies were within \$14,000 of one another in four of the five years, & neither was consistently ahead of the other.

As such, it is fairly evident that employees in smaller companies faced an increasing disadvantage when it comes to salary in the tech industry during this time period. Across the three company sizes, salaries have generally been fairly consistent & therefore predictable aside from the major spike in the salaries of medium-size companies in 2021. While salaries of employees from medium-size & large companies have been relatively comparable as of recent, those from large companies experienced more stability. The only other significant difference between these two larger categories is that medium-size companies offer much higher salaries on the extreme end (up to \$800,000) compared to large companies (up to \\$425,000); however, this could be due to a lack of data on employees from large companies.

Consequently, it could be inferred that having more resources, as larger companies tend to have, is generally more of a benefit for employees in terms of what they earn & for companies in terms of what they can offer. As such, it allows them to more easily attract stronger talent.

Recommendations¶

Of the particular subsets of individuals whose salaries were analyzed, client companies would be advised to offer salaries around or just above the respective averages in order to be more appealing to potential candidates & remain competitive in hiring within the tech industry. In doing so, applicants might be more likely to engage with & pursue job openings at such companies because competitive salaries can make candidates feel that their skills are valued appropriately. If companies offer salaries that are noticeably below average or if they are generally inflexible in what they are willing to offer, individuals might be less inclined to pursue such a job opening & instead look elsewhere.

Among the eight jobs identified in Analysis I that see the highest average salaries, companies will likely need to offer very competitive salaries for such positions. Not only do the responsibilities of these jobs demand higher pay, but the necessity for such candidates to be proficient at handling them do as well. As such, companies looking to fill such positions would definitely be encouraged to pay above average for such jobs.

When analyzing reported salaries based on how much people work remotely, the average salary of people who worked evenly between remote & non-remote work was sizably less than that of people who worked fully remotely or fully in person. Such findings might be indicative of hiring preferences within the tech industry in that companies prefer employees to either fully work in person or fully remotely. Typically, people who do not work remotely are the most expensive. As such, if companies are capable, hiring more remote employees might be more beneficial than hiring mostly in-person employees; however, potential effects of doing so should be taken into account such as the importance of having a lively, in-person working environment & having easy, face-to-face communication & interactions.
When it comes to hybrid work, companies in the tech industry are able to offer considerably less in salary to such employees relative to those who work entirely in person or remotely. Regardless, companies would still be encouraged to pay slightly above average to attract the best talent. For companies specifically looking to hire hybrid employees, they might be more motivated to offer greater salaries given how uncommon such employees are according to the survey responses. For employees, finding jobs in which they can work both remotely & in person will not only be considerably more difficult given how less popular they are, but finding decent salary offers will also be fairly challenging.

Given that smaller companies were found to offer employees considerably smaller salaries than larger companies, specifically those with at least 50 employees, it is reasonable to assert that working in a larger company generally relates to having a larger salary within the tech industry. Once the number of employees exceeds 50, this trend is not necessarily true, nor does it resume at a specific point beyond. As a result, smaller companies will likely need to be prepared to discuss such salaries with potential candidates, particularly that they will likely see a smaller salary than what they might expect depending on the position. To combat such challenges, such companies may need to utilize additional tools to persuade candidates to work for them such as other benefits. For companies that have 50+ employees, they generally are less restricted in what salaries they can offer, so the same general advice could be utilized as mentioned previously--offer slightly more than average to attract the best candidates & remain competitive within the industry.

Analysis I - Highest-Paying Jobs¶

Create a bar chart displaying the top 5 job titles with the highest average salary (in USD).

By identifying the jobs with the highest average salary, it can provide salary expectations for companies when looking to hire certain positions & how expensive they might be relative to other jobs.

When evaluating these jobs, it would useful to get an idea as to the distribution. If one job title has a very high average salary but there are only a couple of corresponding records, then it may not be very representative. As such, a threshold as to how many corresponding records job titles have may need to be applied when investigating those with the highest average salaries.

In [3]:
#obtain summary statistics of "salary_in_usd" per "job_title"
q1_data_I = salaries_df.groupby('job_title').salary_in_usd.describe().reset_index()
#round salaries to 2 decimals
q1_data_I.iloc[:,2:] = round(q1_data_I.iloc[:,2:], 2)
#convert the "count"s to integers
q1_data_I['count'] = q1_data_I['count'].astype('int')

display(q1_data_I.sort_values('count', ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True).head(5))
#inspect distribution of job frequencies

In the dataset, there are 253 unique job titles. 20 of them only account for one data point, whereas the most popular job--data scientists--accounts for 9,706 records. Most of the jobs that are present account for between three & 50 observations each. This information is prevalent because some jobs with few observations may not possess a sufficient, representative number of data points when evaluating which have the largest average salaries. For instance, if a certain job has three survey responses with reported salaries of \$1,000,000, \\$250,000, & \$100,000, the average salary would be \\$450,000; however, these salaries are so inconsistent with one another that they don't provide a reliable, central idea as to what salary such a position might be expected to typically have.
On the other hand, metrics of jobs with many observations will be more diluted & less prone to influence from extreme values. Without normalized data, calculating aggregate statistics like an average can involve biases.

As an alternative to retrieving the jobs with the greatest average salary, jobs with too few observations could be ignored from this process so those that are more representative can be identified; however, it should be noted that outliers do exist in many real-world datasets & applications. In this case, given the number of records per job in this dataset, a better range would include jobs that have at least three records which is the 25th percentile of counts of "job_title"s. Of the 253 unique jobs, 56 of them have less than three unique survey responses (~ 22%); however, these 56 jobs only account for 92 survey responses.

For simplicity, two processes were utilized. 1) Find the jobs with the top average salaries across the entire dataset. 2) Of jobs with at least two records, find the jobs with the top average salaries across the entire dataset.

Analysis I - Highest-Paying Jobs - Conclusions¶

Of the 57,194 survey responses, the jobs with the highest average salaries were identified to get a basic understanding as to which positions are the highest paying. To account for less-than-representative job titles, two methods were employed to obtain these job titles.

Firstly, the five jobs with the greatest average salaries across all of the responses were identified & examined. They included (from highest to lowest): Analytics Engineering Manager, Data Science Tech Lead, Applied AI ML Lead, Head of Machine Learning, & Engineering Manager. Their average salaries ranged between \$262,000-\\$400,000. The first three titles had either one or two records each, & so it is difficult to weigh the reliability of these numbers. The latter two had nine & 268 data points respectively, so they are relatively more representative.

Second, the five jobs with the greatest average salaries of those with at least three survey responses were retrieved & analyzed. They included (from highest to lowest): Head of Machine Learning, Engineering Manager, Head of AI, Machine Learning Model Engineer, & Director of Machine Learning. Their average salaries ranged between \$242,000-\\$289,000. While the Head of Machine Learning sees the highest average salary of these jobs, they also see the smallest outright salary & the most volatility. As such, estimating salaries of Machine Learning Heads may be more challenging. The job with the most consistent salaries of these five positions is the Machine Learning Model Engineer. Overall, the more consistent the salaries of these positions, the more reliable & predictable they are for companies who may be looking to hire such positions.

Across both of these methods, there were some commonalities in the positions. Firstly, two of the jobs--Head of Machine Learning &Engineering Manager--directly overlapped. Additionally, of these eight positions, seven of them refer to titles that directly oversee & direct other employees such as managers, leads, heads, or directors. Moreover, three of them relate to engineering, four relate to machine learning (ML), & two relate to artificial intelligence (AI).
As such, managerial jobs across these three fields appear to be particularly specialized & therefore command higher levels of pay within the tech industry.
Such jobs are likely to be very competitive because companies will want to make sure that candidates are fully capable & worthy of positions that involve many responsibilities. As a consequence, companies should be willing to offer strong salaries to candidates whom meet their satisfaction in the hiring process.

Analysis II - Remote Work & Average Salary¶

Compare the average salaries for employees working remotely 100%, 50%, and 0%. What patterns or trends are present?

With continuing developments in technology, the ability for people to work fully remotely & remain effective has become more accessible. Although fully-remote work may impact work within the office building of a company or business, such as ease of communication & working environment, this style of work can also improve accessibility for both companies & employees in terms of who they can hire & where they can work respectively. In hiring employees who work fully remotely, companies can have a wider range of candidates whom they can choose from to fill positions. For hybrid work, employees still need to be near their office & so hiring such candidates will still be as restricted as those who work fully in person.
Ultimately, whether companies prefer fully-remote or in-person work will depend on various factors, but hybrid work will likely require additional resources & levels of accessibility because companies will have to handle people who work both in the office & from home. As such, hybrid work may be less desirable for businesses.

By evaluating salaries of employees in the tech industry according to how much they worked remotely, it may provide insights as to how prevalent or accessible remote work has become in recent years. If salaries differ, then it may indicate that most companies generally prefer specific types of remote work. As a consequence, employees who may be more restricted to certain types of remote work may face limitations in what salaries they might see. Such information can be relevant to employees &/or companies for which remote work is a factor in the jobs they seek & hire for respectively.

In this dataset, the 'remote_ratio' variable quantifies the percentage of work that an employee does remotely. The survey responses contain three ratios: zero, fifty, & one-hundred percent. To begin, it would be useful to check how many survey responses associate to each of these three ratios to determine a base level of representativeness & credibility of subsequent analyses & findings.

Analysis II - Remote Work & Average Salary - Conclusions¶

Of the 57,194 survey responses, salaries were analyzed according to how much remote work employees did which was described using three remote ratios. Employees either worked only remotely, never worked remotely (in person), or worked evenly between remote work & non-remote work (hybrid). Through analyzing salaries across these remote ratios, trends & differences were obtained that might be indicative as to how popular these three types of work have been & what consequences they might associate with.

Although there were considerably large sample sizes of responses across all three remote ratios, only 271 responses correspond to hybrid employees, whereas the other two ratios each accounted for at least 12,500 responses. Such an imbalance could point to preferences among companies who hire such individuals & the tech industry in general in that hybrid work is not really offered. Alternatively, it could point to a bias in the people who were surveyed in that hybrid workers were not represented equally.

Otherwise, aggregating average salaries revealed a considerable discrepancy between the remote ratios. Specifically, hybrid workers reported salaries (~ \$80,000) that were typically about half of those of either in-person or fully remote employees (~ \\$160,000 & \$150,000 respectively). Such an imbalance may be related to a hiring preferential of companies in that they want candidates to fully commit to one way or the other when it comes to remote work.

Annual analyses were also conducted to further explore these salaries. At the beginning of the five-year period, the average annual salaries of the three remote-work types were somewhat comparable in that they were within about \$30,000 of each other; however, by 2024, this difference had grown beyond \\$80,000. In particular, average salaries of fully remote & in-person employees grew significantly, whereas that of hybrid employees actually decreased by about \$5,000. More specific changes are listed below.

  • People who did not work remotely earned about \$94,000 in 2020 & \\$164,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$70,000.
  • People who worked evenly between remote & in-person work earned about \$87,000 in 2020 & \\$82,000 in 2024 which is a decrease of about \$5,000.
  • People who only worked remotely earned about \$115,000 in 2020 & \\$152,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$37,000.

As such, it is quite evident that in-person work became increasingly more valuable over these five years. Fully remote work also saw an increase in value but not quite to the same extent. Hybrid work, on the other hand, saw a small decrease in value from 2020-2024. Consequentially, it could be surmised that tech companies generally prioritized in-person & fully remote positions significantly more than hybrid positions. Furthermore, hybrid employees seemingly would generally have had, & might in the near future, more difficulty in obtaining a hybrid position that pays well.

Analysis III - Company Size & Salary¶

Visualise the salary distribution (in USD) across company sizes (S, M, L). Which company size offers the highest average salary?

The size of a company is generally based on the resources at its disposal. Larger companies tend to have a wider sphere of influence & accessibility, more offices & locations, more employees, & they tend to produce more whether it in the form of products, impact, or money. Regardless, the amount of money in salaries being paid to employees will increase for larger companies because they naturally have more employees that they need to pay. While larger companies may have more money to pay more employees, individuals may see smaller salaries depending on how many there are & how much a business is making.
By evaluating reported salaries across different company sizes, it could provide an indication as to what kind of balance between employees & business output/production is generally more desirable for companies.

In the survey, company sizes were paritioned into three groups based on how many employees worked at a business. Small ("S") companies had less 50 employees, medium ("M") companies had between 50-250 employees, & large ("L") companies had more than 250 people. Similarly to Analysis II, it would be useful to check how many survey responses associate to each of these three company sizes to determine a base level of representativeness & credibility of subsequent analyses & findings.

A significant majority of the survey responses (55,025) correspond to medium-size companies, whereas only 204 associate with small companies.

Generally speaking, salaries are competitive for employees in medium-size & large companies given that they are around the overall average reported salary (~ \$159,000) of the 57,194 survey responses. In particular, medium-size companies typically offer the highest salaries (~ \\$160,000), but those of large companies are not far off (~ \$153,000). Small companies, however, offer relatively uncompetitive salaries (~ \\$88,000) that are roughly half of those of medium-size & large companies.
When examined across the entire distribution, reported salaries of employees from small & large companies are fairly similar (\$15,000-\\$420,000), whereas the largest salaries of people from medium-size companies are significantly greater (~ \$800,000). As such, salaries of medium-size companies are the least predictable; however, this may be a consequence of the severe imbalance in the survey responses across the three company sizes.

As such, it seems that employees in medium-size companies are generally valued the most across the three company sizes. Moreover, employees who work in small companies appear to be valued significantly less than those who work in medium & large companies. It should be noted that there are considerably fewer records in the dataset of employees who work in small companies than others so the imbalance in the survey responses could potentially be a factor in these observed differece. Alternatively, another theory could be that smaller companies are not able to afford their employees as lush of salaries as larger companies because they simply have less resources. Exploration of these metrics over time could help explore these analyses further.

Given these observations, it seems that small companies have a noticeably more challenging time in providing competitive salaries compared to larger companies within the tech industry. It is reasonable to assert that having fewer resources will lead to less production that will result in accruing less profits from which employees can be paid; however, having fewer employees would theoretically help combat this. Smaller salaries will potentially make it more challenging for these smaller companies to attract better talent which could help achieve greater levels of success. With this in mind, smaller companies seem to face multiple challenges compared to larger companies within the tech industry beyond just salaries they offer their employees.
To further explore these differences, salaries can be analyzed over time.

The plot above displays the annual average salary reported by employees within the tech industry between 2020-2024 according to their company size. For reference, small companies were defined to have less than 50 employees, medium-size companies have between 50-250 employees, & large companies have more than 250 employees.

The annual average salary across each company size saw a generally linear, positive trend over the five-year period, but there are some important disparities. At the beginning of the period, the average salaries of the three company sizes were within \$37,000 of each other. Come 2024, this difference had grown to beyond \\$70,000. Conversely, the difference in average salary of employees from medium-size & large companies was no more than \$14,000 in four of the five years, an indication as to their similarity. While the average salary of those from large employees steadily increased year over year, employees from medium-size companies saw a considerable drop from 2020 to 2021 (nearly \\$30,000); however, their average salary increased every year thereafter. For those from small companies, not only did their average salary decrease annually between 2021-2023, but the largest increase between years was only about \$13,000. Smaller companies just weren't able to match the increasing salaries that were seen in larger companies.

  • People who worked in small companies earned about \$77,000 in 2020 & \\$93,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$16,000.
  • People who worked in medium-size companies earned about \$113,000 in 2020 & \\$161,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$48,000.
  • People who worked in large companies earned about \$114,000 in 2020 & \\$165,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$51,000.

As such, it is fairly evident that employees in smaller companies faced an increasing disadvantage when it comes to salary in the tech industry during this time period. While salaries of employees from medium-size & large companies have been relatively comparable as of recent, those from large companies experienced more stability. Across the three company sizes, salaries have generally been fairly consistent & therefore predictable aside from the major spike in the salaries of medium-size companies in 2021.
Consequently, it could be inferred that having more resources, as larger companies tend to have, is more of a benefit for employees in terms of what they earn & for companies in terms of what they can offer. As such, it allows them to more easily attract stronger talent. To determine whether medium-size or large companies are more preferable, it would be beneficial to have a better understanding as to the exact employee count given that these categories are directly adjacent. For instance, if most survey responses from a medium-size company worked at a business with a certain number of employees (or a small range), then it might indicate that salary offers generally stop differing once a company reaches a certain capacity. Determing whether that would be due to more restricted resources or companies making decisions as to how much they are willing to offer would require more data.

Analysis III - Company Size & Salary - Conclusions¶

Of the 57,194 survey responses, salaries were analyzed according to how the size of the company employees worked at. Companies were labeled as either small (less than 50 employees), medium (between 50-250 employees), or large (more than 250 employees). Through analyzing salaries across these company sizes, trends & differences were obtained that might be indicative as to how capable &/or conservative companies were when it comes to providing competitive salaries.

Although there were considerably large sample sizes of responses across all three remote ratios, only 204 responses correspond to employees from small companies, whereas medium-size companies account for more than 55,000 of the responses. Such an imbalance could give a general indication as to the size of most companies within the tech industry. Alternatively, it could point to a bias in the people who were surveyed in small & large companies were not represented equally.

Otherwise, aggregating average salaries revealed a considerable discrepancy between the company sizes. Specifically, employees from small companies reported salaries (~ \$88,000) that were typically about half of those from either medium-size or large companies (~ \\$160,000 & \$153,000 respectively). Such an imbalance may be related to hiring capabilities of companies, their resources, & how they chose to allocate them when it comes to the salaries of their employees.

Annual analyses were also conducted to further explore these salaries. At the beginning of the five-year period, the average annual salaries of the three remote-work types were somewhat comparable in that they were within about \$37,000 of each other; however, by 2024, this difference had grown beyond \\$70,000. In particular, average salaries of employees from medium-size & large companies grew considerably, whereas those of employees from small companies only increased by about \$16,000. Moreover, average salaries of those from medium-size & large companies were within \\$14,000 of one another in four of the five years, & neither was consistently ahead of the other. More specific changes are listed below.

  • People who worked in small companies earned about \$77,000 in 2020 & \\$93,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$16,000.
  • People who worked in medium-size companies earned about \$113,000 in 2020 & \\$161,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$48,000.
  • People who worked in large companies earned about \$114,000 in 2020 & \\$165,000 in 2024 which is an increase of about \$51,000.

As such, it is fairly evident that employees in smaller companies faced an increasing disadvantage when it comes to salary in the tech industry during this time period. Across the three company sizes, salaries have generally been fairly consistent & therefore predictable aside from the major spike in the salaries of medium-size companies in 2021. While salaries of employees from medium-size & large companies have been relatively comparable as of recent, those from large companies experienced more stability. The only other significant difference between these two larger categories is that medium-size companies offer much higher salaries on the extreme end (up to \$800,000) compared to large companies (up to \\$425,000); however, this could be due to a lack of data on employees from large companies.

Consequently, it could be inferred that having more resources, as larger companies tend to have, is generally more of a benefit for employees in terms of what they earn & for companies in terms of what they can offer. As such, it allows them to more easily attract stronger talent. To determine whether medium-size or large companies are more preferable, it would be beneficial to have a better understanding as to the exact employee count given that these categories are directly adjacent. For instance, if most survey responses from a medium-size company worked at a business with a certain number of employees (or a small range), then it might indicate that salary offers generally stop differing once a company reaches a certain capacity. Determining whether that would be due to more restricted resources or companies making decisions as to how much they are willing to offer would require more data. Given that the most extreme salaries for medium-size companies were so much higher than large companies, it could possibly indicate that large companies are more conservative as to the ceiling in what they offer.
